ReleaseLabel: Set 108 'Three-Module Pipeline Tutorial', Session 4 of 4: the human walk of docs/tutorials/three-module-pipeline.md
Notes:
This is the acceptance test for Set 108. Four items, one per part, because the tutorial's whole claim is that each part is finishable on its own.

WHAT IS ALREADY PROVEN, SO YOU DO NOT HAVE TO CHECK IT. Session 4 walked all four parts and built all three services from the contract sections alone. The mechanics hold: every documented response body came back byte-identical, the two-value repoint changed zero code files, and the whole thing was driven against the published answer key's services to prove two independent implementations interoperate. That evidence is in s4-walk-evidence.md.

WHAT ONLY YOU CAN ANSWER, AND THE REASON THIS EXISTS. That walk was PARTIAL, in one specific and important way: it never ran the Dabbler lifecycle the tutorial routes every part through -- `Dabbler: New Module`, the Work Explorer, and the plan-set -> decomposition-set -> implement sequence. It wrote the code directly instead. So the engineering is proven and THE PRODUCT WORKFLOW ON THE MAIN PATH IS NOT. Add to that: the walk was done by an AI, on the machine the tutorial was written on, so it could not measure how long a PERSON takes and could not feel a stall. Those are the deliverables here.

THE CLOCK IS THE POINT. Note the time you start each part and the time you reach its finish line. Per-part time matters far more than a total: the tutorial sells itself as 'a course, not a sitting', and if a part cannot be finished in one go that claim is false and we need to know.

THE NUMBERS ARE THE DELIVERABLE, NOT THE PASS. A part that takes three hours and says so is worth more than one reported as fine. Nothing downstream needs a particular answer.

STOP BETWEEN PARTS ON PURPOSE -- TWICE. Close the laptop after Part A, and again after Part B, and come back another day each time if you can. Those two stops are not a courtesy to your schedule, they are the test: the tutorial claims four independently resumable parts, and the walk could only prove that nothing is left running. Whether YOU can pick it up cold from the document alone is the half nobody has answered, and it is items 2 and 3.

Passes: false means NOT YET WALKED, not 'failed'.

You do not need to grade the writing. If a line made you re-read it, guess, or go looking elsewhere, put it in that item's Feedback -- that is a stall, and a stall is a defect in the tutorial, not in you. If nothing did, leave it empty.

Review.Subarea: Prerequisites on a machine that is not the author's, and three modules in the tree
Review.ItemLabel: A reader with the two documented installs can declare three modules and see them in the Work Explorer
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: a machine that is NOT the one this tutorial was written on, with VS Code, the Dabbler extension, and a repository you already took through Adopt Dabbler (so one module is already declared).

1. Note the time.
2. Open docs/tutorials/three-module-pipeline.md and follow 'Before you start' -- run both checks it gives you:
     dotnet --list-sdks
     sqllocaldb info
3. Do what the SDK callout tells you about global.json.
4. Read 'The two contracts' through once. Do not skim it -- everything later depends on it.
5. Follow Day one, Steps 1-3. Run Dabbler: New Module three times, then Dabbler: Open modules.yaml and add the code roots.
6. Look at the Work Explorer. Note the time.
Review.Expectation:
dotnet --list-sdks prints a line beginning '10.0.'.

sqllocaldb info prints:
  MSSQLLocalDB

After step 3, dotnet --version prints the 10.0.x version you pinned.

The Work Explorer shows FOUR module rows: the one you already had, plus 'Converter (<you>)', 'Persistence (<you>)' and 'Watcher (<you>)' -- your three together, in the order you declared them, each with no session sets under it yet. No warnings, and your original module still there.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: Session 4 drove the day-one manifest through the shipping readModulesManifest / classifyModulesManifest / computeVisibleModules: classification 'present', four entries in manifest order, all four 'declared', zero fallbacks, zero warnings. NOT VERIFIED: the `Dabbler: New Module` command itself was never run -- the manifest entries were written by hand in the exact shape the extension emits -- and no human has looked at the Work Explorer. Both are yours to exercise.

Review.Subarea: One module, built from a contract, then a clean stop
Review.ItemLabel: A reader can hand the contract to their own agent, reach the finish line, and walk away
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: day one is committed and pushed. Nothing is running.

1. Note the time.
2. Follow Part A: open your converter module and run its plan set, then its decomposition set, then implement -- giving your agent Contract 1 as the tutorial says to.
3. Run your tests.
4. Start the service and run the two commands the finish line gives you, substituting your own name:
     dotnet run --project modules/<you>/converter --urls http://localhost:5101
     curl.exe -s -F "file=@samples/orders.csv;type=text/csv" -F "schema=orders" http://localhost:5101/convert
     curl.exe -s -F "file=@samples/orders-invalid.csv;type=text/csv" -F "schema=orders" http://localhost:5101/convert
5. Note the time. THEN STOP -- close everything and come back another day.
Review.Expectation:
Your tests are green. The count will NOT be 31 and does not need to be.

The first curl returns a body that begins:
  {"schema":"orders","sourceFile":"orders.csv","rowCount":3,"rows":[{"OrderId":1001,

The second returns a body that begins:
  {"title":"The CSV file did not match the schema.","schema":"orders","sourceFile":"orders-invalid.csv","errors":[{"line":2,

If 'dotnet run' says it could not find a project, that is expected and the tutorial tells you what to do; note whether its instruction got you moving.

When you come back, Part A needs nothing running and nothing remembered.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: Session 4's converter, built from Contract 1 alone, returned both bodies BYTE-IDENTICAL to the strings printed in the tutorial (379 and 421 chars), 29 tests green. NOT VERIFIED, and this is the biggest single gap in the machine walk: THE DABBLER LIFECYCLE THIS PART OPENS WITH -- run its plan set, then its decomposition set, then implement -- WAS NEVER RUN. The code was written directly instead. You are the first person to exercise that sequence here, so a stall anywhere in it is a genuine finding, not you doing it wrong.

Review.Subarea: A second module, a real stop in the middle, then one that composes both
Review.ItemLabel: A CSV's rows reach a database, the reader can stop after Part B and resume cold, and the decision table was proven before anything was wired up
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: Part A is finished and behind you.

1. Note the time. Follow Part B and reach its finish line -- post the same batch twice.
2. Note the time. This is Part B's number on its own; keep it separate from Part C's.

3. NOW STOP, AND THIS STEP IS AS MUCH THE TEST AS ANYTHING ELSE. Close every terminal, shut down anything still running, close the repository and walk away. Come back on a different day if you possibly can -- a few hours at the very least. Do not re-read your notes when you return; use only the tutorial.

4. Back cold, note the time. Read Part C's 'Coming back to this?' line and get yourself going from that alone.
5. Follow Part C, PHASE A ONLY: build the decision table and its tests. Do not start any service.
6. With nothing running at all, run your watcher tests.
7. Follow Phase B: create the drop folder, start all three services, drop samples\orders.csv and then samples\orders-invalid.csv under new names, and call:
     curl.exe -s -X POST http://localhost:5103/run-now
8. Note the time.
Review.Expectation:
Part B: the second post returns "duplicate":true carrying the SAME batchId as the first. If it returns a new one, say so -- that is the failure this part exists to catch.

Coming back at step 4: everything you built in Parts A and B is still there and still works -- you should not have to rebuild, re-migrate, re-seed or redo anything. If you could not work out where you were from the tutorial alone, SAY SO IN FEEDBACK: that is the single most important thing this item can tell us, and it is the one thing the machine walk could not test.

Phase A: your watcher tests pass with no database, no services and nothing else started. All four outcomes are covered: Stored, AlreadyStored, Rejected, Deferred.

Phase B: the good file comes back "outcome":"Stored" and its rows read back out of the database; the bad file comes back "outcome":"Rejected" and is sitting in the failed\ folder while the good one is in archive\.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: Session 4: persistence 29 tests green, the documented 400 envelope byte-identical, duplicate rule held first try. Watcher 26 tests green in 54 ms with both services confirmed DOWN by curl -- and that suite caught a real bug in its first run. The MACHINE half of the Part B stop was then exercised: with everything stopped, persistence was cold-started and a batch stored during Part B read back intact, still returning its original batchId as a duplicate. NOT VERIFIED, and this is why step 3 exists: whether a PERSON can resume from the document alone after a real gap, and how long Parts B and C take them.

Review.Subarea: The payoff -- two strings, no code
Review.ItemLabel: A reader's watcher drives a second set of services after changing two configuration values and nothing else
Review.HumanAction:
Where you are: Part C works against your own three services.

1. FIRST, PIN A BASELINE -- the acceptance test at step 5 is worthless without one. From your repository root:
     git add -A
     git commit -m "part C finished"
     git rev-parse HEAD
   Write that commit id down. It is called PARTC below.
2. Note the time.
3. Follow Part D. If a teammate's modules are merged and pulled, use theirs. If not, use 'If you are working alone' and run a second copy of your own two services on the 52xx band.
4. Change the two BaseAddress values, restart your watcher, drop a CSV under a new name and run:
     curl.exe -s -X POST http://localhost:5103/run-now
   Then read the batch back through the service on 5202, using the id it gave you.
5. NOW THE ACCEPTANCE TEST. Run this from your repository root, substituting the commit id you wrote down, and paste what it prints:
     git add -A
     git diff --cached --name-only PARTC -- "*.cs" "*.csproj" ":(exclude)*/bin/*" ":(exclude)*/obj/*"
6. Note the time.
Review.Expectation:
Step 4: the run returns "outcome":"Stored" and the batch reads back out of the service on 5202 with your three orders in it.

Step 5 prints NOTHING AT ALL. That is the acceptance test for this whole tutorial: if it lists even one file, Part D failed and something upstream is coupled that should not be.

Do not shorten that command. `git add -A` first is what stops a new source file hiding as untracked; comparing against PARTC is what stops a change hiding by having been committed; and the two exclusions keep generated build output under bin/ and obj/ from producing a false failure.
Review.ProgrammaticVerification: Session 4 ran exactly this check on the walk repository: 0 files. The complete source diff across the whole Part D range is one file, watcher/appsettings.json, with no untracked source. The check was also confirmed to be a REAL falsifier rather than one that happens to return zero -- planting a single line in DecisionTable.cs made it appear immediately. Part D was then repeated against the PUBLISHED ANSWER KEY's converter and persistence, a genuinely independent implementation, which also worked. Not verified: whether a real second person's modules, merged and pulled, behave the same.
